title: Auray-Blais (Jan 2003 TCC) Tax Court of Canada Ruling
subject: TCC informal-procedure appeal on whether a used tractor was an SR&ED capital expenditure and how partnership losses were split.
outcome: Appeals dismissed; the tractor was an SR&ED capital expense but not ITC-qualified property (used), and the 90/10 loss split stood.
summary: Auray-Blais v. The Queen (TCC), sometimes labelled a 2003 decision but dated January 8, 2002, held that a tractor bought by two Quebec research partners was an SR&ED capital expenditure under section 37 of the Income Tax Act, yet not ITC-qualified property because it was previously used, and upheld their 1997 90/10 partnership loss split as reasonable.
metaDescription: Discover the January 2003 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Auray-Blais and its impact on Canadian R&D tax credit claims.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Auray-Blais v. The Queen (Dockets 2000-3931(IT)I and 2000-3934(IT)I, heard on common evidence in Sherbrooke, Quebec, on September 5, 2001, and rendered on January 8, 2002, by the Honourable Judge Louise Lamarre Proulx; some Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) jurisprudence databases and file copies label the case with a January 2003 date, but the judgment itself is dated and signed January 8, 2002) stands as an instructive judicial precedent governing the eligibility of capital equipment and the allocation of partnership business losses within scientific research enterprises. Heard under the Informal Procedure of the Tax Court of Canada, the joint appeals involved two spouses and research partners, Christiane Auray-Blais and Jean-François Blais, who contested reassessments issued by the Minister of National Revenue (the Minister) dated May 8, 2000, in respect of the 1996 and 1997 taxation years.
The Taxpayers' Claims

During the 1996 and 1997 taxation years, Christiane Auray-Blais—a biochemist employed at the Centre Hospitalier de l'Université de Sherbrooke (CHUS), where, according to the Minister's technical adviser, she worked on a full-time basis in 1997—and Jean-François Blais, also a biochemist, were partners in an unincorporated business engaged in SR&ED in the province of Quebec, whose research project (which the Minister did not dispute was an SR&ED activity) concerned the development of hops and barley plants capable of resisting certain diseases and infections. In computing their net income and tax payable, the appellants advanced two primary tax positions on their personal income tax returns. First, for the 1996 taxation year, the appellants included in their SR&ED expenditure account under section 37 of the Canadian Income Tax Act (the Act) an amount of $36,000 for the acquisition of a tractor that had previously been used for two years but was sold with a new-tractor warranty, and claimed a corresponding Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act; for the 1997 taxation year, the disputed SR&ED item was an interest expense of $5,410 on loans that included a $33,000 loan to purchase a Landini tractor. Christiane Auray-Blais testified that they had purchased one tractor in 1997 and another, reconditioned tractor in 1996, that they had bought the tractor to do the cultivation work required for SR&ED activities in an experiment that might last 10 to 15 years, and that she would not have acquired the tractor had it not been for research and development projects; the appellants argued that the tractor would be used 100 percent for SR&ED and that its useful life would coincide with the anticipated duration of their project. Relying on the broad purposive principle articulated by Judge Hamlyn in Com Dev Ltd. v. Canada, [1999] T.C.J. No. 141 (Q.L.)—which cited Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen for the proposition that section 37 of the Act is designed to encourage scientific research in Canada—the appellants argued for a liberal construction of capital equipment eligibility.

Second, the appellants contested the Minister's reallocation, on an equal 50/50 basis, of their partnership's business loss for the 1997 taxation year, which they had reported with only 10 percent of the loss allocated to Jean-François Blais. According to Jean-François Blais's calculations filed in evidence (Exhibit A-1), for the years 1994 to 1997 his salary had ranged from 88 percent to 12 percent of the salary of Christiane Auray-Blais, and in 1997 her income was double his; these figures describe the spouses' relative incomes, not fluctuating partnership loss allocations. For the 1997 taxation year specifically, the appellants contended that Jean-François Blais was simultaneously participating in two research projects—that of the partnership and that of a corporation, Innovations et Intégrations Brassicoles Inc.—so that Christiane Auray-Blais had devoted many more hours to the joint project (508 hours versus 51 hours, according to their compilation) and, because each partner had contributed in proportion to income, more financial resources as well.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister disallowed the 1996 tractor ($36,000) both as an SR&ED expenditure and for the ITC, disallowed the 1997 interest expense of $5,410 as an SR&ED deduction and for the ITC (as a prescribed expenditure under section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations), and, relying on subsection 103(1.1) of the Act, reassessed the partnership loss allocation on an equal 50/50 basis between the two partners for the 1997 taxation year. In challenging the capital equipment claim, the Crown's witnesses raised several objections at the hearing, although the only reason actually communicated to the appellants and pleaded in the Reply to the Notice of Appeal was that the tractor's useful life was longer than the duration of the SR&ED project. The Canada Customs and Revenue Agency (CCRA) regional scientific adviser, Jean-Guy Paquet, expressed the view that the purchase of the tractor was excessive for the research purposes pursued, comparing it to the purchase of a Boeing aircraft by a person experimenting with the surfacing of airstrips. He also testified that the tractor could not be considered a capital expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED because the tractor itself was not subject to experimentation and was not a prototype used in the SR&ED activities. The auditor, Gaétan Descheneaux, testified that the project's lifetime was 10 years and the tractor's lifetime 20 to 25 years, the report on objection noted a dealer's estimate that a 10-year-old tractor of the same make would sell for approximately $20,000 (concluding that 90 percent of the tractor would not have been consumed after 10 years of SR&ED), and certain witnesses also expressed the opinion that the tractor was not used during all or substantially all of its operating time in SR&ED activities.

With respect to the sharing of the partnership's business losses, the Minister's position was that at no time had the appellants been able to provide documents proving the allocation of work time between the partners, and the report on objection confirmed the 50/50 sharing because there was no document proving that one partner had worked 90 percent of the time and the other only 10 percent. The fact that Jean-François Blais's second research project in 1997 belonged to an incorporated company came from his own testimony: a $15,000 National Research Council grant had been awarded to the corporation, which paid him that amount as salary. The Minister's technical adviser, Bertrand Provencher, testified that in 1997 Christiane Auray-Blais worked at CHUS on a full-time basis while Jean-François Blais worked on his own research project, that it was therefore reasonable to believe the two worked equally on the partnership's project, and that, the partners' financial contributions not having been specifically revealed, there was no reason why the sharing would not be 50/50; Counsel for the Respondent separately argued that the proportion in which the tractor was used for the partnership's project was vague, given Jean-François Blais's other research project and the appellants' farming activities.
Governing Statutory Framework and Final Holding

The legal dispute centered on the statutory interplay between section 37, subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III), the definitions of "qualified expenditure" and "qualified property" in subsection 127(9), subsection 127(5) and section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations, alongside subsection 103(1.1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), which governs the reasonableness of income and loss sharing between non-arm's-length partners. Under the statutory regime in force during the 1996 and 1997 taxation years (before capital expenditures were excluded from SR&ED for property acquired after 2013, an exclusion reversed for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024), capital expenditures qualified as SR&ED expenditures under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) only if, at the time the expenditure was incurred for the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment, it was intended either that the property would be used during all or substantially all (generally interpreted by the CRA as 90 percent or more, the threshold applied in the Minister's report on objection) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or that all or substantially all of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of such SR&ED. Satisfying the requirements of subsection 37(8) was necessary but not sufficient to earn an ITC under subsection 127(5): as the Court held, the tractor also had to meet the separate subsection 127(9) definition of "qualified property", which requires that the property not have been used, or acquired for use or lease, for any purpose whatever before it was acquired by the taxpayer, and a current expenditure such as interest that is a prescribed expenditure under section 2902 of the Regulations is not a "qualified expenditure" even if it is an SR&ED expenditure under section 37.

Judge Lamarre Proulx did not uphold the Minister's primary positions on either the eligibility of the tractor as an SR&ED capital expenditure or the 50/50 allocation of the partnership's 1997 business losses: she held that the 1996 acquisition of the tractor is an expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED within the meaning of subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III), and that the appellants' agreement concerning the sharing of profits and losses for 1997 was reasonable. The Court did not rule that "useful life" means economic life; that statement, together with the evidence that the economic life of a tractor is usually 15 to 20 years and that a tractor does not lose much value, came from the testimony of CCRA appraiser Marcel Vaillancourt, and the Court instead confined itself to the only reason given to the appellants and stated in the Reply—that the tractor's useful life exceeded that of the project—criticizing the Minister for failing to state in the Reply, or communicate to the appellants, the figures relied on (a possible residual value of $20,000 and some 10 years of remaining operating life) and observing that it was not clear at first glance that substantially all of the tractor's value would not be consumed by the end of a 10-to-15-year project. Consequently, because the appellants' proposal was not, on its face, unreasonable as regards the useful life of the tractor, and because the respondent had not pleaded any of the other arguments raised by its witnesses (excessiveness, substantial non-SR&ED use, or unreasonableness of the expenditure), the Court concluded that the tractor was a capital expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED; however, because the tractor had been used for two years before the appellants acquired it, it was not "qualified property" for the ITC under subsection 127(9), notwithstanding its new-tractor warranty. On the partnership issue, the Court applied subsection 103(1.1) and held that, in view of the financial contributions made (each partner having contributed in accordance with income, and the partners' incomes differing greatly) and the work performed (Christiane Auray-Blais having devoted her free time and summer vacation to research and many more hours than her husband, who had his own research project), the appellants' income sharing agreement for 1997 was reasonable in the circumstances; the Court noted that the Minister's agents had not seen an itemized account of contributions or hours, but that no letters specifically requesting such information were in evidence. The appeals were allowed, without costs, and the assessments referred back to the Minister for reconsideration and reassessment on that basis, with the further conclusion that the 1997 interest expense of $5,410 was an SR&ED expenditure within the meaning of paragraph 37(8)(a) but, being a prescribed expenditure under section 2902 of the Regulations, was not qualified for the ITC.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Issues

A rigorous legal and technical analysis of Judge Lamarre Proulx's reasons for judgment shows that the taxpayers in fact prevailed on the central section 37 and partnership-sharing issues and lost only on two narrow ITC points (the used tractor and the prescribed interest expense); the five themes below are therefore best read as the statutory, technical, contractual, and evidentiary risk areas raised by the evidence and by the Crown's arguments, several of which failed for procedural reasons (lack of pleading and of communication to the taxpayers) rather than on their merits.
The "All or Substantially All" Useful Economic Life Test (Where the Minister's Objection Failed)

The Minister's primary position in Auray-Blais, as pleaded in the Reply, was that the tractor's useful life was longer than the duration of the SR&ED project; the appellants answered that the tractor was used 100 percent for SR&ED and that its useful life would coincide with the anticipated 10-to-15-year duration of their project, at the end of which it would no longer be of any use. Christiane Auray-Blais testified that she would not have acquired the tractor "had it not been for research and development projects". The Court did not decide the case on that motivation; it framed the test as requiring that, at the time the capital expenditure is incurred, the equipment either be intended for use all or substantially all of the time for SR&ED during all or substantially all of its normal operating time, or that all or substantially all of its value be intended to be consumed in SR&ED activities.

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III), the relevant question is what was intended at the time the expenditure was incurred regarding the equipment's use during all or substantially all of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. The statement that "useful life means economic life" was made by CCRA appraiser Marcel Vaillancourt in his testimony; Judge Lamarre Proulx did not adopt it as a legal holding. The evidence on useful life was in fact contested: the appraiser said the economic life of a tractor is usually 15 to 20 years, the auditor put the tractor's lifetime at 20 to 25 years against a 10-year project lifetime, and the appellants testified that their project could last 10 to 15 years and that the tractor would have no remaining value or use at its end. Because the Minister's specific figures on useful life and residual value were neither stated in the Reply nor transmitted to the appellants, because the appellants' proposal was not, on its face, unreasonable, and because no other arguments had been pleaded, the Court concluded that the acquisition of the tractor was a capital expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED within the meaning of paragraph 37(8)(a) of the Act.
Value Consumption and the Distinction Between Object and Tool of Experimentation (Not Decided Against the Taxpayers)

The second branch of subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) permits a capital expenditure to qualify if it was intended that "all or substantially all of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of scientific research and experimental development in Canada". As the Minister's witness, regional scientific adviser Jean-Guy Paquet, observed, the tractor itself was not subject to experimentation and was not a prototype used in the SR&ED activities; the Court, however, did not base its decision on this view. The statement that "[a] tractor does not lose much value" was testimony from CCRA appraiser Marcel Vaillancourt, not a matter of which Judge Lamarre Proulx took judicial notice.

On value consumption, the Court held that it is not clear at first glance that substantially all of the value of a tractor would not be consumed in SR&ED activities at the end of a 10-to-15-year project, and that specific data (such as the dealer's $20,000 estimate for a 10-year-old tractor recorded in the report on objection) must be stated in the letters to the taxpayers and in the Reply so that a valid and fair debate may be conducted in Court. The regional scientific adviser also described the purchase of the tractor as clearly excessive for the research purposes pursued by the appellants; the Court noted that this might be a valid reason but declined to consider it because it was not the reason given to the appellants or stated in the Reply (short-term equipment leasing or custom service contracting is a practical alternative suggested by this analysis, not by the Court). The capital outlay therefore qualified under subsection 37(8); what barred the 1996 ITC was that the tractor had been used for two years before the appellants acquired it, so that it was not "qualified property" within the meaning of subsection 127(9), the Court finding the text of the Act "quite clear" on this point despite the new-tractor warranty.
Over-Reliance on Purposive Statutory Interpretation Over Explicit Statutory Conditions

In paragraph 27 of the judgment, the appellants relied on Judge Hamlyn's decision in Com Dev Ltd. v. Canada (which in turn cited the Tax Court of Canada's decision in Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 DTC 724) for the principle that section 37 of the Act is designed to encourage scientific research in Canada, and they argued that its provisions are measures to encourage research that must be liberally interpreted.

The Auray-Blais ruling underscores a critical doctrinal boundary in Canadian SR&ED tax litigation. While the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal generally apply a purposive approach when evaluating the scientific and technological eligibility criteria of the SR&ED definition (in subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations for the years in issue, now in subsection 248(1) of the Act), and the appellants succeeded under subsection 37(8) itself, purposive interpretation could not override the clear, unambiguous conditions of the "qualified property" definition in subsection 127(9) or of section 2902 of the Regulations. As Judge Lamarre Proulx concluded, relying on Judge Mogan's decision in Minicom Data Corp. and Judge Kempo's decision in Spectron Computer Corp., the language of Regulation 2902(a)(i) is clear and unequivocal, so the $5,410 interest expense—although an expenditure of a current nature attributable to SR&ED under section 37—was a prescribed expenditure and therefore not a qualified expenditure for the ITC; likewise, the requirement that qualified property not have been used for any purpose before acquisition could not be relaxed on the basis of the general pro-research policy of section 37.
Partnership Loss Allocations Under Subsection 103(1.1) (Upheld as Reasonable)

Under the Civil Code of Québec provisions governing contracts of partnership and the federal Income Tax Act, partners generally enjoy broad contractual freedom to stipulate how the profits and losses of a partnership business will be shared. However, as set out in paragraphs 42 and 43 of the decision, subsection 103(1.1) of the Act provides that where non-arm's-length partners agree to share income or loss in proportions that are not reasonable in the circumstances, having regard to the capital invested in or work performed for the partnership or other relevant factors, the share is deemed to be the amount that is reasonable in the circumstances.

The 88-to-12-percent figures in the evidentiary record do not describe loss allocations: they are Jean-François Blais's calculation that, from 1994 to 1997, his salary ranged from 88 percent to 12 percent of the salary of Christiane Auray-Blais, and the Court drew no inference of retroactive personal tax minimization from them. For the 1997 taxation year, the appellants argued that Christiane Auray-Blais should be allocated more than 50 percent of the partnership's business loss because Jean-François Blais had his own separate research project during that year. Judge Lamarre Proulx accepted this contention: although the Minister's technical adviser had testified that Christiane Auray-Blais worked at CHUS on a full-time basis in 1997 while Jean-François Blais worked on his own research project, the Court found that she devoted her free time and summer vacation to research, that the appellants had explained the difference in the number of hours worked (508 hours versus 51 hours in their compilation), and that they had contributed financially in accordance with their greatly differing incomes. The Court therefore held that the 1997 income sharing agreement was reasonable in the circumstances and did not uphold the Minister's 50/50 reallocation, while noting that the Minister's agents had not seen an itemized account of financial contributions or hours and that no letters requesting such information were in evidence; the absence of day-to-day work descriptions and of tables of each partner's financial contributions nonetheless remained an evidentiary weakness in the appellants' record.
Separate Corporate Personality in Project Attribution

During his testimony concerning the 1997 taxation year, Jean-François Blais explained that he was participating in two research projects: that of the partnership and that of Innovations et Intégrations Brassicoles Inc. The evidence established that the second research project belonged to a distinct corporation—to which the National Research Council awarded a $15,000 grant that the corporation paid to Jean-François Blais as salary—and not to Jean-François Blais personally or to the spousal partnership.

Under Canadian corporate and tax law, an incorporated company possesses a separate legal personality distinct from its shareholders, directors, and officers. As a general principle, SR&ED activities, expenditures, or time commitments undertaken within a corporate project accrue to the corporation and should be kept distinct from an individual partner's work for an unincorporated partnership. In Auray-Blais, however, the Court did not treat the corporate project as improper commingling or as damaging the appellants' credibility; it accepted Jean-François Blais's work for the corporation (2,300 hours in 1997, against 51 hours on the joint project) as a legitimate explanation for his smaller contribution to the partnership, while Counsel for the Respondent's argument that the tractor was also used for the corporation's research and for farming activities was not decided because it had not been pleaded in the Reply.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and legal requirement examined in Auray-Blais v. The Queen against the taxpayers' position (and, where applicable, their actual evidentiary or legal failure) and what the Tax Court of Canada actually decided.

Tax Court of Canada Decision and Standard Applied

cells: Capital Equipment Operating-Time Threshold ("All or Substantially All")
Income Tax Act, s. 37(1)(b) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III)

No failure found: the appellants argued that the tractor would be used 100% for SR&ED over a 10-to-15-year project coinciding with its useful life; the 15-to-20-year economic-life figure came from the CCRA appraiser and was not pleaded in the Reply.

The Court did not hold that "useful life" means economic life. It looked at the intention at the time the expenditure was incurred and required the Minister to state in the Reply and in letters to the taxpayers the specific facts relied on (useful life, residual value); absent such allegations, the appellants' proposal was not unreasonable and the tractor qualified under s. 37(8)(a).
Capital Equipment Value-Consumption Alternative
Income Tax Act, subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III)

No failure found: the Court held that it was not clear at first glance that substantially all of the tractor's value would not be consumed by the end of a 10-to-15-year project; the $20,000 residual-value estimate appeared only in the report on objection and was never communicated to the appellants.

Where the Minister relies on residual value, specific data must be pleaded and communicated so that a valid and fair debate can take place. An asset retaining substantial residual value may fail the value-consumption test if the Minister properly pleads and proves it, but that was not done here.
Qualification for Investment Tax Credits (ITCs)
Income Tax Act, ss. 127(5) and 127(9) ("qualified expenditure" and "qualified property"); Income Tax Regulations, s. 2902

The 1996 tractor had been used for two years before acquisition, so it was not "qualified property" despite its new-tractor warranty; the 1997 $5,410 interest expense was a prescribed expenditure under s. 2902 of the Regulations.

Qualification under s. 37(8) does not by itself confer an ITC. Qualified property must not have been used, or acquired for use or lease, for any purpose before acquisition, and current expenditures described in Reg. 2902(a)(i), including interest under s. 20(1)(c), are prescribed expenditures that are not qualified expenditures under s. 127(9).
Scope of Purposive Interpretation in SR&ED Claims
Com Dev Ltd. v. Canada, [1999] T.C.J. No. 141; Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen (T.C.C.)
Invoked the general pro-incentive purpose of s. 37 to support a liberal interpretation; this succeeded on the s. 37 issue, but could not overcome the clear wording of s. 127(9) and Reg. 2902.

While s. 37 is designed to encourage scientific research in Canada, purposive construction cannot override clear, unambiguous statutory language—here the s. 127(9) "qualified property" definition and Reg. 2902 (Minicom Data Corp.; Spectron Computer Corp.).
Partnership Business Loss Allocation
Income Tax Act, s. 103(1.1)

No failure found: the 88% and 12% figures were Jean-François Blais's salary as a percentage of Auray-Blais's salary (1994–1997), not loss allocations; for 1997 the appellants reported a 90/10 split supported by testimony of 508 versus 51 hours and income-proportional financial contributions.

Under s. 103(1.1), sharing between non-arm's-length partners must be reasonable having regard to capital invested, work performed and other relevant factors. The Court found the 1997 agreement reasonable and did not uphold the Minister's 50/50 reallocation, despite the absence of day-to-day records and contribution tables.
Entity-Level Attribution of R&D Projects
Corporate personality principles; Income Tax Act, s. 37(1)

Not a failure: Jean-François Blais's 2,300 hours on the project of Innovations et Intégrations Brassicoles Inc. (which received a $15,000 NRC grant paid to him as salary) were accepted as explaining his limited hours on the partnership's project.

The Court made no ruling on entity segregation; separate corporate personality is a general principle, and the corporate project was simply not the project in issue. The Crown's argument that the tractor was also used for the corporation's work and for farming was not decided because it was not pleaded.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

Informal asset acquisition and retrospective loss allocation routinely result in audit disallowances by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Although Parliament amended paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act to exclude capital expenditures and capital lease costs from federal SR&ED deductions and ITCs for property acquired after 2013, and the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, assented to March 26, 2026) restored that eligibility for property acquired, and lease costs incurred, on or after December 16, 2024, the principles applied by Judge Lamarre Proulx in Auray-Blais—the need for the Minister to plead and communicate the specific facts relied on, the strict "unused property" requirement for qualified property, the prescribed-expenditure exclusion for interest, and the subsection 103(1.1) reasonableness test for partnership allocations—remain relevant in contemporary Canadian SR&ED practice. Specifically, tax advisors and claimants can use the facts and arguments in Auray-Blais to distinguish ineligible multi-purpose capital equipment from eligible materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) or eligible arm's-length SR&ED subcontracts, as well as to structure research partnerships and multi-entity corporate groups where principal investigators hold concurrent institutional appointments (such as university or hospital chairs).

The following two applied industry case studies demonstrate step-by-step how Canadian taxpayers facing the legal and evidentiary risks raised by the Crown in Auray-Blais (several of which the Court did not decide because they had not been pleaded) can restructure their project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to anticipate those objections and fully satisfy statutory SR&ED requirements.
Case Study 1: AgTech and Forestry Bioprocessing — Overcoming the Multi-Purpose Machinery and "Value Consumption" Trap
Industry Scenario and Initial Vulnerability

Boreal Phytogenetics S.E.N.C. is a Quebec-based general partnership formed by two biochemical engineers to develop a novel enzymatic soil-inoculation and high-pressure mechanical root-injection process designed to accelerate secondary metabolite synthesis in northern coniferous saplings. To conduct field trials over two growing seasons (16 months total), the partnership plans to acquire a specialized $185,000 commercial forestry tractor and pneumatic root-seeder unit.

If Boreal Phytogenetics purchases this $185,000 commercial forestry tractor unit outright and attempts to claim the outlay as an SR&ED expenditure or material cost, the claim will fail—unlike the appellants in Auray-Blais, whose 1996 tractor was accepted by the Court as an SR&ED capital expenditure under the pre-2014 rules and failed only for ITC purposes because it had previously been used. Although the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3) restored the eligibility of capital expenditures for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, a capital expenditure enters the SR&ED expenditure pool and ITC calculations only if, when it is incurred, the equipment is intended to be used during all or substantially all of its operating time in its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or all or substantially all of its value is intended to be consumed in such SR&ED, under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III), and a commercial tractor deployed in a 16-month trial cannot plausibly meet either test. Furthermore, even if the partnership attempts to characterize the machinery or its heavy mechanical attachments as "materials consumed or transformed" in the prosecution of SR&ED under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) or 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), the CRA can be expected to rely on the kind of evidence its witnesses gave in Auray-Blais—an appraiser's testimony that a tractor's economic life is usually 15 to 20 years and that a tractor does not lose much value, and a scientific adviser's view that the tractor was not the object of experimentation and that its purchase was excessive—arguments that, if properly pleaded and communicated, would be especially strong against a 16-month project. It is an enduring capital support tool, not a consumed material.
Step 1: Project Governance — Segregating the Experimental Prototype Subsystem from the Commercial Carrier Vehicle

To establish an audit-proof claim, Boreal Phytogenetics must institute a formal engineering and financial governance protocol prior to procuring any assets. The project steering committee must explicitly divide the physical architecture of the field apparatus into two distinct accounting and engineering categories. The first category is the Non-Experimental Carrier Platform, consisting of the standard commercial tractor that merely provides mechanical locomotion and hydraulic power across the forest test plots; the governance charter must strictly prohibit the partnership from claiming the acquisition or lease cost of this commercial tractor as an SR&ED expenditure. The second category is the Experimental Custom Injection Manifold, comprising the custom-engineered high-pressure enzymatic injection nozzles, peristaltic metering chambers, and biodegradable polymer delivery conduits that are physically subjected to destructive wear, chemical corrosion, and iterative structural failure during testing. By drawing a bright governance line between the commercial carrier vehicle and the custom experimental subsystem, the taxpayer prevents the CRA from tainting the entire mechanical budget as an excessive capital acquisition.
Step 2: Contractual Restructuring — Replacing Capital Acquisition with Arm's-Length Custom Field-Operation Subcontracts and Destructive Prototype Fabrication

Rather than purchasing a $185,000 tractor with a typical 15-to-20-year economic life (according to the CCRA appraiser's testimony in Auray-Blais), Boreal Phytogenetics must restructure its commercial contracts along two distinct statutory pathways under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 127(9) of the Act. First, to obtain the necessary field locomotion without acquiring capital property or entering into an equipment lease whose cost would itself have to meet the "all or substantially all" requirements of subsection 37(8), Boreal executes a formal Arm's-Length SR&ED Support Services Contract with an independent Quebec forestry contractor. Under the Statement of Work (SOW), the contractor provides a tractor and operator strictly on an hourly fee-for-service basis (for example, 140 hours across the two growing seasons at $160 per hour, totaling $22,400) to pull Boreal's custom injection manifold across the designated experimental test beds in accordance with Boreal's test protocols. The contract explicitly stipulates that Boreal acquires zero proprietary, leasehold, or possessory interest in the tractor, and that the contractor is remunerated solely for performing direct physical support work in Canada that is commensurate with the engineering requirements under paragraph (d) of the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Act. Under subsection 127(9), 80 percent of this arm's-length contract payment qualifies for SR&ED ITCs.

Second, for the custom enzymatic injection manifold, Boreal executes procurement contracts and machine-shop fabrication orders for raw stainless-steel billets, piezoelectric micro-valves, and elastomeric seals ($38,000 total). The purchase orders and engineering work authorizations explicitly state that these raw materials are acquired solely for transformation into three iterative experimental manifold prototypes that will be destructively tested to structural failure under acidic enzyme pressure cycles, thereby consuming more than 90 percent of their economic value and rendering them non-reusable scrap.
Step 3: Technical Documentation — Framing the Technological Uncertainty Around the Consumed Prototype Materials

In drafting the CRA Form T661 (Part 2) technical narrative, the tax advisor must ensure that the commercial tractor is never presented as the subject of the SR&ED project. Instead, the technical documentation must define the Technological Uncertainty strictly around the fluid-dynamics and metallurgical interface of the custom manifold: specifically, whether high-viscosity enzymatic suspensions can be injected at pressures of up to 2.5 MPa into heterogeneous boreal subsoils without shear-induced denaturation of the enzyme macromolecule or cavitation-induced micro-fissuring of the nozzle orifices. The Technological Advancement must be articulated as the generation of new engineering knowledge quantifying the relationship between nozzle geometry, elastomeric damping, and enzymatic survival rates above 92 percent at the root cortex interface.
Step 4: Experimentation and Consumption Tracking

To meet the kind of value-consumption and operational-dedication evidence that the Minister's witnesses relied on in Auray-Blais—and that the Court held must be specifically alleged and communicated so it can be fairly debated—Boreal Phytogenetics must maintain a dual tracking system throughout the 16-month project. For the custom manifold materials, the engineers must compile Destructive Testing and Scrap Disposition Logs, including dated high-resolution photographs of cavitated nozzles, pressure-cycle failure telemetry, and third-party scrap-metal weight receipts proving that the transformed materials retained zero commercial or residual value (≥ 90% value consumed) at the conclusion of the trials. For the subcontracted tractor operations, the project manager must maintain Contemporaneous Field-Run Logs counter-signed daily by the lead researcher and the third-party operator, cross-referencing every billed hour of tractor support to a specific experimental run number, soil-pressure hypothesis, and GPS test-plot coordinate.
Case Study 2: Biomedical Diagnostics Partnership — Overcoming Institutional Employment Overlap, Entity Commingling, and Partnership Loss Reallocation
Industry Scenario and Initial Vulnerability

Dr. Hélène Savard (a full-time clinical biochemist and medical genetics researcher employed at a university teaching hospital in Sherbrooke, Quebec) and Marc-Antoine Savard (an analytical instrumentation specialist) form an unincorporated Quebec general partnership, Labo-Spectra Enr., to develop a high-throughput tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) multiplex screening assay for rare metabolic biomarkers. Simultaneously, Marc-Antoine is the sole shareholder and director of SpectraSoft Inc., a separate corporation developing chromatography peak-integration algorithms.

In Year 1, Labo-Spectra Enr. incurs $120,000 in deductible SR&ED expenditures (resulting in a net business loss of $120,000) and generates $18,000 in federal ITCs. Because Dr. Savard earns $210,000 in full-time hospital employment income while Marc-Antoine draws no salary from SpectraSoft Inc., the couple files their personal T1 income tax returns allocating 90 percent of Labo-Spectra's business losses and ITCs to Dr. Savard and 10 percent to Marc-Antoine, asserting that Marc-Antoine was occupied with SpectraSoft Inc.'s corporate research project during Year 1.

Auray-Blais v. The Queen does not dictate that this structure will be rejected—in that case the Court accepted a 90/10 loss split for 1997 under subsection 103(1.1) even though Christiane Auray-Blais was employed at CHUS, because she devoted her free time and summer vacation to the joint project and the partners contributed financially in proportion to their very different incomes—but the CRA is likely to reassess it, and the taxpayers will have to defend it, on three grounds. First, as the Minister's technical adviser argued about Christiane Auray-Blais, the CRA may contend that Dr. Savard's full-time hospital employment makes it implausible that she contributed 90 percent of the operational labour to the partnership while her partner contributed only 10 percent; in Auray-Blais that argument failed on the taxpayers' testimony, but the absence of day-to-day work records and contribution tables left them exposed to a contested hearing. Second, under subsection 103(1.1) of the Income Tax Act (with subsection 103(1) separately addressing agreements whose principal reason may reasonably be considered to be the reduction or postponement of tax), a non-arm's-length partner's share of partnership losses may be deemed to be the amount that is reasonable having regard to capital invested, work performed and other relevant factors; in Auray-Blais the Court held a 90/10 allocation reasonable on those factors, so a well-documented asymmetric allocation can survive, while an undocumented one remains at risk of a 50/50 reassessment. Third, any research activity conducted by Marc-Antoine on SpectraSoft Inc.'s project legally belongs to the corporation, not to Marc-Antoine personally or to the partnership, although—as in Auray-Blais, where Jean-François Blais's 2,300 hours on a corporation's project explained his small partnership share—time spent on the corporation's project can legitimately explain a smaller contribution to the partnership.
Step 1: Corporate and Partnership Governance — Eliminating Unincorporated Partnership Ambiguity via Incorporation or Capital-Tracked Partnership Deeds

To eliminate the structural vulnerabilities highlighted by the Minister's challenge in Auray-Blais, the taxpayers must overhaul their organizational governance before incurring SR&ED expenditures. The preferred structural remedy is Corporate Consolidation into a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC): the partners should dissolve the unincorporated partnership (or roll its assets into a corporation under subsection 85(2) of the Act) and conduct all SR&ED within a single CCPC, such as Labo-Spectra Inc. Conducting SR&ED inside a CCPC entitles the corporation to the enhanced 35 percent refundable federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit under subsection 127(10.1) of the Act (as well as Quebec's refundable R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act (Quebec)), delivering immediate cash refunds directly to the corporation without needing to flow business losses through to Dr. Savard's personal T1 return or navigate the restrictive partnership ITC allocation rules of subsection 127(8).

Alternatively, if commercial or regulatory considerations require retaining the unincorporated Quebec general partnership (société en nom collectif), the partners must execute a formal, written Contract of Partnership prior to the commencement of the fiscal year. To withstand challenge under subsection 103(1.1) of the Act—which deems the share of non-arm's-length partners to be the amount that is reasonable having regard to capital invested, work performed and other relevant factors—the partnership agreement must establish a fixed, non-discretionary formula tying profit, loss, and ITC allocations directly to audited partner capital contributions and contemporaneous labour hours, expressly prohibiting retroactive annual adjustments; if financial contributions are to track the partners' incomes, as the Court accepted in Auray-Blais, that formula should be stated in advance rather than applied after the fact to Dr. Savard's external hospital salary.
Step 2: Contractual Terms — Institutional Intellectual Property Waivers and Inter-Entity Service Agreements

To neutralize the institutional-employment and corporate-commingling risks raised by the Minister's witnesses in the Auray-Blais proceedings, the taxpayers must execute two binding legal instruments. First, Dr. Savard must secure a formal Extramural Research and Intellectual Property Waiver signed by the authorized technology-transfer officer of the university teaching hospital. This agreement must certify that Dr. Savard's work for Labo-Spectra is performed strictly outside her full-time hospital employment hours, utilizes no unbilled hospital personnel or grant funding, and vests 100 percent of the resulting intellectual property and commercial exploitation rights in Labo-Spectra. If Labo-Spectra requires access to the hospital's tandem mass spectrometers during off-peak hours, Labo-Spectra must execute a written Arm's-Length Analytical Sample Processing Agreement with the hospital's research centre, paying a documented per-sample analytical fee rather than attempting to claim hospital equipment as partnership capital property.

Second, to respect the separate corporate personality of SpectraSoft Inc., Labo-Spectra and SpectraSoft Inc. must execute an explicit Inter-Entity Research Boundary and Subcontracting Agreement. Under this contract, SpectraSoft Inc.'s peak-integration software project is legally, financially, and technically segregated from Labo-Spectra's biochemical assay project. Any software development performed by Marc-Antoine for SpectraSoft Inc. is accounted for exclusively on SpectraSoft Inc.'s T2 corporate return and Form T661, and is never cited as a factor in determining Labo-Spectra's internal partnership allocations.
Step 3: Technical Documentation — Segregating Project Boundaries Across Entities on Form T661

To prevent the CRA from alleging project duplication or commingling across the hospital, the partnership, and the corporation, each taxpayer entity must prepare a rigorously bounded Form T661 technical submission. Labo-Spectra's Form T661 must restrict its Technological Uncertainty and Work Performed strictly to the wet-lab clinical biochemistry challenges: specifically, overcoming matrix effects, ion suppression, and in-source fragmentation interferences when eluting multiplex metabolic biomarkers from dried biological specimens using novel mobile-phase modifiers. Conversely, SpectraSoft Inc.'s Form T661 must restrict its technical narrative strictly to the mathematical and algorithmic uncertainty of real-time deconvolution of overlapping isotopic isomers in noisy spectrometric data streams. Furthermore, Labo-Spectra's technical dossier must include an appendix mapping its experimental objectives against Dr. Savard's published hospital grant proposals, proving zero overlap between her publicly funded CHUS/hospital research and Labo-Spectra's private commercial SR&ED.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Time and Capital Contribution Tracking

To meet the Tax Court of Canada's evidentiary burden regarding partner contributions and defeat a Ministerial reallocation to 50/50 under subsection 103(1.1), the partners must implement rigorous financial and time-tracking controls. Both Dr. Savard and Marc-Antoine must maintain Comprehensive Daily Timesheets signed weekly, accounting for 100 percent of their professional working hours across all three spheres of activity: (1) Dr. Savard's full-time hospital duties (e.g., 37.5 hours/week), (2) Marc-Antoine's corporate duties for SpectraSoft Inc. (e.g., 25 hours/week), and (3) each partner's exact evening and weekend hours devoted to Labo-Spectra's experimental runs (e.g., 15 hours/week each).

Because their operational labour contributions to Labo-Spectra are equal (15 hours/week each), any allocation of losses and ITCs exceeding 50 percent in favour of Dr. Savard must be anchored in Verified Partner Capital Contributions. Rather than paying partnership invoices informally from personal bank accounts, Dr. Savard must transfer her personal after-tax funds into a dedicated Labo-Spectra partnership bank account, recorded contemporaneously in the partnership's general ledger as formal paid-in capital pursuant to the written Partnership Agreement. By substantiating both the exact parity of labour hours and the documented asymmetry of at-risk capital contributions through audited partnership financial statements, the taxpayers establish the objective evidentiary foundation required by the Tax Court of Canada to sustain their claimed allocations under the Income Tax Act.
